## Why
I chose a lion’s head sculpture, cast in dark, patinated bronze and positioned as if roaring, to embody Leo XIII's *Etsi Nos*. This single, powerful figure represents both the Pope himself (Leo) and the 'Lion of Judah,' capturing the courageous, urgent spirit the encyclical demands from Italy's clergy and faithful when facing the "pernicious sect." While the text includes specific imagery of chains or siege, a dynamic lion—specifically a non-abstract, classical zoomorphic figure—is the most recognizable archetypal subject that translates the encyclical’s entire call for bold spiritual action and resistance into a cohesive, non-composite form.

## Why
I chose a roaring lion's head in patinated bronze as the single sculptural subject to translate *Etsi Nos*. This figure directly embodies the courage, strength, and defensive vigilance that Pope Leo XIII ("the lion") calls for from the bishops and faithful in the face of an aggressive, hostile force (the "pernicious sect") that has attacked the Church and "imprisoned" him. By opting for a dynamic, roaring posture rather than a passive one, it captures the active resistance, formation of associations, and renewal of action Leo demands. A single, recognizable creature is far more concrete and legible as a symbol of courageous defense and spiritual authority than a building or a scene of conflict, maintaining the strict requirement for a single, unified, non-abstract subject.
